lesson.title: The Network Edge: Where Hosts Meet the Network
lesson.summary: Defines the network edge as the outer portion of the network made up of hosts and the access links that connect them, distinguishing it from the switching interior covered next.
lesson.body:
Every network has a shape, and one useful way to describe that shape is to split it into two regions: an edge and a core. The network edge is the outer region, made up of the hosts, the end system nodes covered earlier such as laptops, phones, and servers, together with the access links that connect each of those hosts into the rest of the network. If you picture the internet as a large, tangled structure, the edge is everything sitting at the outside boundary of that structure: the devices people actually use and the first link each one takes to reach everything else.

The access link is the crucial piece that makes the edge more than just a list of devices. When your laptop connects over WiFi to a home router, or when a data center server connects through a cable to a switch, that connection is the access link, the specific communication link that attaches a host to the network. Access links vary enormously in speed and technology: home internet connections, corporate office cabling, and cellular data connections are all different kinds of access links doing the same fundamental job, getting a host's data onto the network and, on the way back, delivering data to that host.

The edge is deliberately defined in contrast to the network core, discussed in the next section, which is made of the routers and switches that interconnect everything once traffic leaves the edge. This split is useful because the two regions have very different jobs and very different design concerns. At the edge, the priority is connecting individual hosts, potentially billions of them, each with its own access link, often over the last mile of cabling or wireless spectrum closest to the user. In the core, the priority is efficiently routing enormous volumes of aggregated traffic between many different edges at once.

Consider tracing a request from your laptop to a distant web server as a worked example. Your laptop, a host at the edge of the network, connects over an access link, your home WiFi, to your home router. That router connects, over another access link, to your internet service provider. From there, the request leaves the edge entirely and travels through the network core, discussed next, before eventually arriving at the destination web server's own access link, which connects that server, another host at the edge, to its network. Notice that the journey begins and ends at the edge, at the two hosts with something to say, while everything in the middle belongs to the core.

Recognizing the edge as a distinct region of the network helps explain design choices you may already have noticed, why home internet plans emphasize the speed of your specific access link, and why network engineers spend so much effort on the last mile problem of connecting individual homes and businesses. All of that effort is about building and improving the network edge.
